strengths: Solid theoretical contribution: the paper derives a clean self-consistency property for the diffusion-bridge control drift in terms of the Jacobian (derivative) process, and proves a sharp characterization (Theorem 3.1) showing the diffusion bridge is the unique bridging, gradient-form process satisfying this property. Full proofs are given in the appendix, including a generalized version with a change-of-measure argument to control Jacobian blow-up.

The resulting algorithm avoids backpropagation through simulated trajectories (unlike the main competitor NGDB), yielding a substantial wall-clock speedup (~3.5x in the OU experiment) while achieving comparable or better KL divergence to the ground-truth bridge in several settings.

Thorough set of experiments spanning multiple regimes: OU bridges (closed-form ground truth), CIR model (state-dependent diffusion), 1D double-well and cell-differentiation dynamics (non-conservative drift), and a harder 2D Muller-Brown potential inspired by transition-path sampling; comparisons against several recent strong baselines (NGDB, SDB, FB, DL).

Useful ablations on design choices: different alpha-weighting schedules (next-step/average/endpoint), Sticking-the-Landing variance-reduction adjustments, and the generalized self-consistency loss (choice of auxiliary drift b-tilde), with clear discussion of when each choice helps (e.g., avoiding large Jacobian growth near potential peaks).

Nice connections drawn to existing stochastic optimal control frameworks (adjoint matching, SOCM), situating the contribution within a broader theoretical landscape and clarifying novelty relative to Pidstrigach et al. (2025).
weaknesses: Experiments are restricted to low/moderate dimensions (up to d~30 for a simple linear OU process; 1-2D for the more interesting nonlinear/chemistry-motivated examples). The intro motivates applications in chemistry and rare-event sampling, but no genuinely high-dimensional or realistic molecular system is tested, leaving the practical significance and scalability of the method for the stated target applications largely unverified.

The method does not consistently outperform the main baseline NGDB in accuracy -- in several settings (rare-event and multimodal cell-diffusion, Muller-Brown) NGDB is reported as slightly better -- so the central claim is a favorable speed/accuracy trade-off rather than a strict improvement; this trade-off is only quantified with wall-clock numbers in the OU experiment, not across all settings.

The generalized algorithm's key hyperparameter, the auxiliary drift b-tilde (e.g., 0 vs -b), needs to be manually selected per problem to avoid Jacobian explosion (as shown in the double-well and Muller-Brown examples where b-tilde=0 fails or is unstable). No principled, automatic rule for choosing b-tilde is provided, which could limit ease of use in new settings, especially higher-dimensional or more complex potentials where the 'right' choice may not be obvious a priori.

The paper explicitly excludes hypoelliptic diffusions (a common and practically important setting in molecular dynamics with underdamped/Langevin-type dynamics), which is a significant limitation given the chemistry-motivated framing of the introduction.

The main paper is extremely compressed (4 pages of content) with essentially all technical and experimental substance deferred to a lengthy appendix; while the appendix is detailed, this makes the main text alone insufficiently self-contained for assessing the method without extensive cross-referencing.

Additional design choices (alpha-schedule, STL adjustments) each introduce further tuning knobs and computational trade-offs (e.g., STL costs ~1.5x compute for modest gains) without strong theoretical guidance on default settings, somewhat undercutting the simplicity/practicality narrative.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution is non-trivial and rigorously derived: Theorem 2.1 establishes a necessary self-consistency property of the optimal control via the Jacobian/derivative process, and Theorem 3.1 (with the detailed equivalence in Theorem D.2) shows that this property, combined with the gradient-form and bridging constraints, is in fact sufficient to characterise the unique diffusion bridge control. This elevates the method beyond a heuristic loss to one with a clean theoretical justification.

The proposed fixed-point/self-consistency loss avoids backpropagation through simulated trajectories, which is the main scalability bottleneck of the most comparable prior method (NGDB, Yang et al. 2025). The reported wall-clock improvement (230s vs 800s for 5000 steps) is a meaningful practical advantage.

The paper explicitly connects its self-consistency framework to existing stochastic optimal control objectives (adjoint matching, SOCM), showing these can be recovered as special cases, which strengthens the theoretical unification and originality of the contribution.

The generalised self-consistency property (Appendix B.4, Theorem B.1/B.2) addressing Jacobian blow-up in concave/non-convex regions (e.g., double-well, Müller-Brown potentials) is a thoughtful practical extension that retains the theoretical guarantees, and is empirically shown to meaningfully stabilise training in challenging settings.

Reasonably broad empirical validation across five settings (OU bridges, CIR model, double-well potential, cell differentiation process, Müller-Brown potential) with comparisons to several baselines (NGDB, SDB, FB, Doob's Lagrangian) and informative ablations (α-schedules, STL adjustments) in the appendix.
Honest discussion of limitations (ellipticity requirement, need to simulate the current controlled process, sensitivity to the auxiliary drift choice) rather than overstating generality.
weaknesses: The main body is extremely compressed, with most experimental details, quantitative tables, and even some core algorithmic descriptions deferred to the appendix; the self-contained main text provides only one quantitative comparison (OU bridges) and mostly qualitative visualizations for the other settings, making it hard to assess the core claims without the appendix.

Empirical improvements in accuracy over the main competitor (NGDB) are modest and inconsistent: NGDB performs comparably or better in several settings (e.g., cell diffusion rare/multimodal cases, Müller-Brown KL and max energy), so the main claimed advantage is computational efficiency rather than solution quality, but this is not sufficiently emphasized/quantified as the central contribution in the main text.

The generalised algorithm's performance is sensitive to the choice of auxiliary drift (b̃=0 vs b̃=-b), and the paper shows that using the 'wrong' choice can cause outright training failure (e.g., Müller-Brown example). There is no principled or automatic procedure for selecting this hyperparameter in general, which could limit robustness and ease of use in new applications.

The theoretical framework is restricted to elliptic diffusions, excluding hypoelliptic settings common in Hamiltonian/molecular dynamics applications that motivate the work in the introduction; this restricts applicability to some of the stated target domains.

Several of the derivations (e.g., interchanging derivative and expectation via stochastic flows, uniqueness of solutions to the linear parabolic PDE governing vorticity) rely on regularity conditions that are only referenced informally rather than carefully verified for the function classes used in the neural parameterisation.

No clear statement of code/artifact release for the proposed method itself (only licenses for baseline codebases are listed), raising some reproducibility concerns despite fairly detailed algorithmic descriptions.

The writing is dense and notation-heavy throughout.html, which combined with the main text's brevity, may hinder accessibility for readers not already familiar with stochastic flows, Girsanov's theorem, and the SOC literature.

strengths: The core theoretical contribution—a self-consistency property for the optimal control of diffusion bridges expressed via the Jacobian (derivative) process—is rigorously derived (Theorem 2.1) and shown to be both necessary and, combined with gradient-form and bridging constraints, sufficient to characterize the true bridge (Theorem 3.1), with full proofs provided in the appendix.

The proposed fixed-point/self-play style loss avoids backpropagation through simulated trajectories, yielding a meaningful computational speedup over the most comparable baseline (NGDB), e.g. ~230s vs ~800s for 5000 training steps in the OU experiment, while achieving comparable or better accuracy.

The paper identifies a concrete failure mode of the basic method (explosion of Jacobian terms under concave/ridge-like potentials) and derives a principled generalization via a Girsanov change-of-measure argument (Theorem B.1/B.2) that retains the same theoretical guarantees while mitigating this issue in practice (demonstrated on double-well and Müller-Brown experiments).

Experiments span a good range of settings: closed-form OU bridges (varying dimension and OU parameter), CIR model (spatially-dependent diffusion), double-well potential, non-conservative drift (cell differentiation model) in normal/rare/multimodal regimes, and a challenging Müller-Brown transition-path setting, benchmarked against several recent, well-chosen baselines (NGDB, SDB, FB, DL).
Thorough ablations on α-schedules (next-step/average/endpoint) and sticking-the-landing adjustments give practical guidance and show the authors understand variance-bias tradeoffs in their estimator.
The work carefully relates its self-consistency framework to existing stochastic optimal control literature (adjoint matching, SOCM), clarifying how these connect to and generalize prior objectives.
Honest and specific limitations discussion (ellipticity requirement, need to simulate the controlled process during training, instances where NGDB slightly outperforms the method).
weaknesses: The main paper is extremely condensed (4 pages of core content) with most technical details, derivations, and even some key algorithmic descriptions relegated to the appendix; this hurts the self-containedness and readability of the main submission.

Experiments remain fairly low-dimensional and synthetic (OU bridges up to d≈30, 1-2d potentials); there is no demonstration on realistic, higher-dimensional molecular dynamics or scientific applications despite motivating the work with such applications.

The method still requires simulating the current controlled process at every training iteration, and no wall-clock or scaling comparison is given for higher-dimensional or more complex systems beyond the toy benchmarks used.

Performance is not uniformly superior to baselines—NGDB slightly outperforms the proposed method in rare-event and multimodal cell-diffusion settings, and the generalized variant (b̃=-b) sometimes exhibits higher variance across runs (e.g., Müller-Brown KL has larger std than NGDB).

The theoretical guarantee depends on being able to enforce the gradient-form property of the control, which is natural only when the base drift is conservative; the generalization to more complex noise/drift structures is sketched but not deeply explored, and hypoelliptic extensions are left entirely to future work.

Baseline comparisons largely use default hyperparameters from the respective codebases without clear evidence of hyperparameter tuning parity, which could bias comparisons somewhat in favor of the proposed method.

The distinction between necessary (self-consistency alone) and sufficient (self-consistency + gradient-form + bridging) characterization of the solution is subtle and could be made clearer/more accessible in the main text for readers unfamiliar with the stochastic analysis background.
